big_idea: AREA is measured in SQUARE UNITS — cm² for small, m² for big.
learning_intention: We are learning to measure area in square centimetres and square metres.
student_learning_goal: I can measure area in square centimetres and square metres.
success_criteria: I can SAY what cm² means.
I can COUNT cm² inside a shape.
I can PICK cm² or m² for the size.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Roo the Ruler Rabbit — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.

minds_on.hook: Roo: AREA needs a UNIT. We use SQUARE CENTIMETRES (cm²). Count them inside! Roo opens: 'cm² is a TILE — count the TILES!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Roo the Ruler Rabbit puppet with grid paper. 'Measurement friends — yesterday we covered with tiles. Today our tile is OFFICIAL: 1 cm × 1 cm = 1 SQUARE CENTIMETRE = cm².'

Define. 'cm² (square cm) = a square that's 1 cm on each side. Use for small areas like a sticky note.'

Demo. 'Sticky note: 8 cm × 8 cm = 64 cm². Cover with 64 grid squares.'

Then m². 'For big areas like the classroom floor: square metre = 1 m × 1 m. Classroom floor might be 50 m².'

'Roo says — pick the right square unit! cm² for small. m² for big.'

Now estimate. 'Before counting, ESTIMATE.'

Demo. 'Notebook cover. About... 600 cm²? Let's count grid: 26 cm × 21 cm = 546 cm². Close!'

'Roo says — estimate gives a check on your count.'

Now show curved shapes. 'A circle on the grid? Count whole squares + half-squares. About!' Demo a circle covering ~28 squares.

'Roo says — for curved shapes, estimate by counting whole + half squares!'

Now each pair gets cm² grid paper + 4 shape outlines. They count cm² for each.

'Roo says — careful count gives accurate area!'

steps.instruction: Hand out grid paper + shapes. Pairs estimate first, then count cm² for 4 shapes.
For 2 shapes pick cm² or m².
Stretch: count cm² for 1 curved shape (whole + half squares).
STRATEGY COMPARE: Two pairs share L-shape area — one decomposes into two rectangles, one counts tiles. Class compares accuracy. Cite Battista (2007) array structuring vs cell-counting.
steps.teacher_prompt: Roo: 'Same L, two ways. Decompose for SPEED, count for SAFETY.'

differentiation.for_extending: Find area in cm² AND mm² for one shape.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Walk a 1m² square on the floor. NO-PREP PATH: use masking-tape squares on the floor as cm² tiles; children walk the area boundary. Body becomes the tile-counter.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Five signals: estimates; counts; picks unit; handles curves; consistency.

discussion_prompts: When use m² instead of cm²?
consolidation.exit_routine: Roo's cm² chant — 'Roo says: cm² is a TILE — count the TILES!' (3x). Each child reports one shape's area in cm² with the decomposition shown.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child uses cm² for a HUGE area or m² for a tiny one — repairing the unit-size mismatch trap at Grade 3
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On square centimetres + L-shapes, the trap is unit-structuring failure: child applies cm² formula linearly OR fails on L-shape decomposition. Battista (2007) array structuring + Outhred & Mitchelmore (2000) on rectangle-area learning frame this as the Grade-3 area-unit gateway.

Yesterday Lesson 2 introduced rows × columns. Today: standard unit (cm²) and L-shape decomposition. Lesson 4 capacity/mass; Lesson 5 capstones.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Estimate activity. Child writes 'classroom floor = 5 cm²'.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'Roo asks — does 5 cm² fit a CLASSROOM?'

Probe. 'Hold up 1 cm². It's tiny. The floor is HUGE. So pick m² — bigger unit for bigger area.'

Generalise. 'Roo says — match the UNIT to the SIZE. cm² for small. m² for big.'

If still mismatched: physical comparison. '1 cm² (fingernail) vs 1 m² (square on floor).'
common_misconceptions: Bigger number = bigger area. (Repair: depends on unit.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child treats cm² as a length: drill 'square cm = 1 cm × 1 cm = an AREA tile'; physical demo with 1 cm² square.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child can do rectangles but stalls on L-shape: drill 'DECOMPOSE the L into two rectangles; add their areas.'
DIAGNOSTIC C — child decomposes wrong (overlapping): physical cut/paper demo to show non-overlapping rectangle pieces.
